claim: Plectin gene (PLEC) expression is consistently and significantly increased in HCC samples when compared to non-tumor (NT) liver tissues across 17 distinct HCC patient datasets.
source: Using 17 distinct HCC patient datasets, we confirmed that plectin gene (PLEC) expression is consistently and significantly increased in HCC samples when compared to non-tumor (NT) liver tissues (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by meta-analysis of 17 datasets shown in Figure 1A and referenced in the text.

claim: Higher PLEC mRNA levels are associated with a significant decrease in recurrence-free survival in HCC patients.
source: Strikingly, using higher tertile expression as the cut-off, higher PLEC mRNA levels were associated with a significant decrease in recurrence-free survival (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 1B with log-rank test p<0.05.

claim: Quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy of 19 human HCC tissue sections revealed a significant increase of plectin fluorescence intensities in tumor compared to adjacent non-tumor tissue.
source: Consistent with expression analysis, quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy of 19 human HCC tissue sections revealed a significant increase of plectin fluorescence intensities in tumor (T) compared to adjacent non-tumor (NT) tissue, with plectin perimembranous enrichment in tumor hepatocytes (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data from 19 patient samples shown in Figure 1C with paired t-test p<0.001.

claim: Poorly differentiated mesenchymal-like HCC cell lines display elevated plectin levels compared to well-differentiated HCC cell lines.
source: Consistent with mRNA and immunofluorescence analyses, poorly differentiated mesenchymal-like HCC cell lines (characterized by low E-cadherin and high vimentin levels) displayed elevated plectin levels, coinciding with higher migration speed when compared to well-differentiated HCC cell lines (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis and migration assays shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Both quantitative immunofluorescence and immunoblot analyses indicated elevated plectin levels in tumor versus non-tumor liver tissue in DEN-induced murine HCC.
source: Both quantitative immunofluorescence and immunoblot analyses indicated elevated plectin levels in T versus NT liver tissue (Figure 1C, G and H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 1G, p<0.01) and immunoblot (Figure 1H) data from DEN-induced mouse model.

claim: MRI screening 32 and 44 weeks post-DEN injection revealed a significant reduction of tumor number and volume in PlecΔAlb mice compared to Plecfl/fl controls.
source: Remarkably, MRI screening 32 and 44 wk post-injection revealed a significant reduction of tumor number and volume in PlecΔAlb mice compared to Plecfl/fl controls (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by MRI quantification shown in Figure 2A-C with t-test p<0.05.

claim: Decreased tumor burden in PlecΔAlb mice was confirmed macroscopically 44 weeks after DEN administration.
source: Decreased tumor burden in the second cohort of PlecΔAlb mice was confirmed macroscopically 44 wk after DEN administration (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by macroscopic liver analysis shown in Figure 2D and E with t-test p<0.05 and p<0.001.

claim: Plectin inactivation resulted in a reduced number of Huh7 and SNU-475 colonies in a soft agar colony formation assay.
source: Consistent with the murine model, plectin inactivation resulted in a reduced number of Huh7 and SNU-475 colonies in a soft agar colony formation assay, with PST treatment closely mimicking the effect of genetic targeting (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by soft agar assay data shown in Figure 2G with t-test p<0.01 and p<0.001.

claim: Cells with disabled plectin developed significantly smaller subcutaneous xenografts when compared with untreated WT cells.
source: Cells with disabled plectin developed significantly smaller tumors when compared with untreated WT cells (Figure 2H), mirroring the results of the colony-forming assay.
evidence: Supported by xenograft growth curves shown in Figure 2H with two-way ANOVA.

claim: MS-based proteomic analysis found 265 protein groups significantly regulated upon plectin ablation when comparing WT and KO SNU-475 proteomes.
source: We found 265 protein groups significantly regulated (FDR <0.05; s0=0.01) upon plectin ablation when comparing WT and KO SNU-475 proteomes (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by MS-based proteomic analysis with statistical thresholds FDR<0.05, s0=0.01.

claim: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis revealed major plectin-dependent regulation of signaling pathways related to the actin cytoskeleton, such as 'RhoA signaling', 'Actin cytoskeleton signaling', 'Integrin signaling', and 'Signaling by Rho family GTPases'.
source: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) revealed major plectin-dependent regulation of signaling pathways related to the actin cytoskeleton, such as 'RhoA signaling', 'Actin cytoskeleton signaling', 'Integrin signaling', and 'Signaling by Rho family GTPases' (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by IPA analysis of proteomic data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Phosphoproteomic analysis identified 313 regulated phosphosites indicating a major impact on actin, as well as 'ILK signaling', 'FAK signaling', and 'Molecular mechanisms of cancer' among the most altered pathways.
source: Similarly, 313 regulated phosphosites indicated a major impact on actin, as well as 'ILK signaling', 'FAK signaling', and 'Molecular mechanisms of cancer' among the most altered pathways (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by phosphoproteomic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Analysis of proteome differences between WT and PST-treated cells identified abundance changes in 1214 proteins and 326 phosphoproteins.
source: Analysis of proteome differences between WT and PST-treated cells identified abundance changes (FDR <0.05; s0=0.01) in 1214 proteins and 326 phosphoproteins (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by MS-based proteomic analysis with statistical thresholds FDR<0.05, s0=0.01.

claim: Immunoblot analysis revealed that plectin inactivation resulted in considerable changes in expression levels of integrin adhesion receptors (integrins αV and β1) as well as other FA constituents (i.e. talin, vinculin, and paxillin).
source: In agreement with our proteomic analyses, plectin inactivation resulted in considerable changes in expression levels of integrin adhesion receptors (integrins αV and β1) as well as other FA constituents (i.e. talin, vinculin, and paxillin).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Immunoblotting revealed in cells with disabled plectin either generally altered expression (FAK, Akt, Erk1/2, ILK, and PI3K) and/or reduced phosphorylation (Akt, Erk1/2, and PI3K) of key effectors downstream of integrin-mediated adhesion.
source: Moreover, immunoblotting revealed in cells with disabled plectin either generally altered expression (FAK, Akt, Erk1/2, ILK, and PI3K) and/or reduced phosphorylation (Akt, Erk1/2, and PI3K) of key effectors downstream of integrin-mediated adhesion.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3D with statistical significance indicated.

claim: Plectin inactivation in SNU-475 cells produced less delicate vimentin networks compared to WT cells, with filaments often bundled and sometimes collapsing into vimentin clumps.
source: Reminiscent of plectin-deficient fibroblasts (Gregor et al., 2014; Burgstaller et al., 2010), plectin inactivation in SNU-475 cells produced less delicate vimentin networks compared to WT cells, with filaments often bundled and sometimes collapsing into vimentin clumps (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and B, with reference to prior studies.

claim: Quantitative analysis revealed uneven distribution of vimentin filaments throughout the cytoplasm of KO, ΔIFBD, and PST-treated WT cells as evidenced by the distance between the position of the center of vimentin intensity mass and the cell center.
source: A quantitative analysis revealed uneven distribution of vimentin filaments throughout the cytoplasm of KO, ΔIFBD, and PST-treated WT cells as evidenced by the distance between the position of the center of vimentin intensity mass and the cell center (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C with t-test p<0.001.

claim: Plectin-disabled cells showed a dramatic reduction in longitudinal dorsal actin stress fibers and transversal arcs, as well as pronounced ventral stress fibers.
source: In addition to the aberrant vimentin phenotype, we noticed a dramatic reduction in longitudinal dorsal actin stress fibers and transversal arcs, as well as pronounced ventral stress fibers in plectin-disabled cells (Figure 4A, C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 4A, C, and D with t-test p<0.001.

claim: A reduction in F-actin fluorescence intensity was detected in both Huh7 and SNU-475 KO cells.
source: Moreover, we detected a reduction in F-actin fluorescence intensity in both Huh7 and SNU-475 KO cells, as well as a decrease of atomic force microscopy (AFM)-inferred cellular stiffness as a functional readout for a well-formed cytoskeleton (Na et al., 2009; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and F with t-test p<0.001, and referenced to prior study.

claim: A decrease of atomic force microscopy (AFM)-inferred cellular stiffness was detected in plectin KO cells.
source: Moreover, we detected a reduction in F-actin fluorescence intensity in both Huh7 and SNU-475 KO cells, as well as a decrease of atomic force microscopy (AFM)-inferred cellular stiffness as a functional readout for a well-formed cytoskeleton (Na et al., 2009; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: Supported by AFM measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and G with t-test p<0.001, and referenced to prior study.

claim: FAs of micropattern-seeded WT cells were mostly located at the cell periphery, while FAs of plectin-disabled cells were frequently found within the cell interior.
source: Remarkably, while FAs of micropattern-seeded WT cells were mostly located at the cell periphery, FAs of plectin-disabled cells were frequently found within the cell interior (Figure 4A and E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 4A and E with t-test p<0.01 and p<0.001.

claim: Plectin inactivation resulted in an overall reduced number of FAs, and the FAs that remained were larger and more elongated than in WT cells.
source: Moreover, plectin inactivation resulted in an overall reduced number of FAs, and the FAs that remained were larger and more elongated than in WT cells (Figure 4F and G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by quantification of FA number, area, and length shown in Figure 4F, G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, I with t-test p<0.001.

claim: The smaller FAs found in WT cells transmitted significantly higher contractile energy than KO, ΔIFBD, and PST-treated cells.
source: The smaller FAs found in WT cells transmitted significantly higher contractile energy than KO, ΔIFBD, and PST-treated cells, indicating that FAs in plectin-deficient cells were less functional than in WT.
evidence: Supported by traction force microscopy data shown in Figure 4H and I with t-test p<0.05, p<0.01, and p<0.001.

claim: Both Huh7 and SNU-475 cells exhibited a decrease in migration speed upon plectin targeting in the scratch wound healing assay.
source: As anticipated, both Huh7 and SNU-475 cells exhibited a decrease in migration speed upon plectin targeting in the scratch wound healing assay (Figure 5A and B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by scratch wound assay data shown in Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A with t-test p<0.001.

claim: Migrating plectin-disabled SNU-475 cells exhibited more cohesive, epithelial-like features while progressing collectively.
source: It is noteworthy that migrating plectin-disabled SNU-475 cells exhibited more cohesive, epithelial-like features while progressing collectively.
evidence: Observation from scratch wound assay shown in Figure 5A.

claim: WT SNU-475 leader cells were more polarized and found to migrate into scratch areas more frequently than their plectin-deficient counterparts.
source: By contrast, WT SNU-475 leader cells were more polarized and found to migrate into scratch areas more frequently than their plectin-deficient counterparts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B with t-test p<0.001.

claim: Individually seeded SNU-475 cells less frequently assumed a polarized, mesenchymal-like shape upon plectin inactivation in both 2D and 3D environments.
source: Consistent with this observation, individually seeded SNU-475 cells less frequently assumed a polarized, mesenchymal-like shape upon plectin inactivation in both 2D and 3D environments (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by cell shape analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Plectin-inactivated SNU-475 cells exhibited a decrease in N-cadherin and vimentin levels when compared to WT counterparts.
source: Moreover, plectin-inactivated SNU-475 cells exhibited a decrease in N-cadherin and vimentin levels when compared to WT counterparts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C with t-test p<0.05 and p<0.01.

claim: The EGF-guided migration potential of individual KO, ΔIFBD, and PST-treated cells was significantly reduced compared to WT cells.
source: In addition to slower general migration, we also found the epithelial growth factor (EGF)-guided migration potential of individual KO, ΔIFBD, and PST-treated cells to be significantly reduced compared to WT cells.
evidence: Supported by migration tracking data shown in Figure 5D and E with t-test p<0.01 and p<0.001.

claim: Plectin-disabled cells traversed less linear trajectories in both random and directed scenarios.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Gregor et al., 2014), plectin-disabled cells traversed less linear trajectories in both random and directed scenarios (Figure 5D and E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by migration tracking data shown in Figure 5D, E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E with t-test, and referenced to prior study.

claim: Morphodynamic contour analysis revealed a higher protrusion frequency of randomly migrating WT compared to plectin-disabled cells.
source: Our analysis revealed a higher protrusion frequency of randomly migrating WT compared to plectin-disabled cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), while no differences in protrusion orientation were observed (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: Supported by morphodynamic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F with t-test p<0.05, p<0.01, and p<0.001.

claim: Plectin ablation dramatically reduced the capacity of KO and ΔIFBD cells to form stable protrusions in the direction of chemotactic motion.
source: In sharp contrast, plectin ablation dramatically reduced the capacity of KO and ΔIFBD cells to form stable protrusions in the direction of chemotactic motion (Figure 5F–H), although only a marginal effect on the protrusivity was observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by morphodynamic analysis shown in Figure 5F-H with t-test p<0.05, p<0.01, and p<0.001.

claim: In both transwell and spheroid invasion assays, plectin inactivation significantly reduced invasion potential compared to WT cells.
source: In both assays, plectin inactivation significantly reduced invasion potential compared to WT cells (Figure 6A–C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 6A-C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A with t-test p<0.01 and p<0.001.

claim: Plectin-targeted cells degraded dramatically less FITC-labeled gelatin, suggesting that slower invasion is accompanied by defects in ECM degradation.
source: Unexpectedly, plectin-targeted cells also degraded dramatically less FITC-labeled gelatin, suggesting that slower invasion is accompanied by defects in ECM degradation (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by gelatin degradation assay shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B with t-test p<0.001.

claim: High PLEC mRNA expression is associated with advanced TNM stages in an HCC meta-cohort with clinically annotated tumors from HCC patients (n=978).
source: Tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) classification of an HCC meta-cohort with clinically annotated tumors from HCC patients (n=978) demonstrated that high PLEC mRNA expression is associated with advanced TNM stages (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by TNM classification analysis shown in Figure 6F with Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.05 and p<0.01.

claim: Mice receiving WT Huh7 cells succumbed rapidly to disease, while mice receiving KO cells exhibited prolonged survival in the lung colonization assay.
source: Whereas mice receiving WT Huh7 (but not SNU-475; data not shown) cells succumbed rapidly to disease, mice receiving KO cells exhibited prolonged survival (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6G with log-rank test p<0.05.

claim: A prominent reduction in the number and volume of GFP-positive KO- and WT+PST-derived metastatic nodules was found in the lungs 5 weeks post-injection.
source: Although no macroscopic Huh7 nodules were visible, we found a prominent reduction in the number and volume of GFP-positive KO- and WT+PST-derived metastatic nodules.
evidence: Supported by lattice light sheet microscopy quantification shown in Figure 6I with t-test p<0.05, p<0.01, and p<0.001.

claim: MRI analysis at 4, 6, and 9 weeks post-induction revealed that both genetic and pharmacological plectin inactivation results in a substantial reduction in the average tumor number per mouse and the tumor incidence in the Myc;sgTp53 model.
source: Consistent with our in vitro observations, MRI analysis at 4, 6, and 9 wk post-induction revealed that both genetic and pharmacological plectin inactivation results in a substantial reduction in the average tumor number per mouse and the tumor incidence (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by MRI analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Stalled development of PlecΔAlb and PST-treated Plecfl/fl tumors was reflected by a decrease in liver/body weight ratio in a male cohort sacrificed at 6 weeks post-induction.
source: Stalled development of PlecΔAlb and PST-treated Plecfl/fl tumors was also reflected by a decrease in liver/body weight ratio in another male cohort sacrificed at 6 wk post-induction (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: Supported by liver/body weight ratio analysis shown in Figure 7B and C with t-test p<0.05.

claim: Quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy revealed comparable rates of proliferation and apoptosis in Myc;sgTp53-induced tumors across experimental conditions.
source: The quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy revealed comparable rates of proliferation and apoptosis in Myc;sgTp53-induced tumors across experimental conditions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 and TUNEL staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of liver tissue proteomics revealed enrichment in 'PI3K/Akt' or 'Hippo/YAP signaling' pathways upon plectin inactivation.
source: In addition, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA; Subramanian et al., 2005) revealed enrichment in 'PI3K/Akt' or 'Hippo/YAP signaling' pathways (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7D, with reference to the GSEA method.

claim: Through analysis of 1268 HCC patients, gene sets annotated as 'Integrin pathway', 'FAK pathway', 'PI3K Akt/mTOR signaling', or 'Erk pathway' were found to positively correlate with elevated plectin expression.
source: Through analysis of 1268 HCC patients, we found gene sets annotated as 'Integrin pathway', 'FAK pathway', 'PI3K Akt/mTOR signaling', or 'Erk pathway' to positively correlate with elevated plectin expression (Figure 7E; Figure 7—figure supplement 2C; Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E and supplementary figures.

claim: Plectin is a major cytoskeletal crosslinker protein that plays a crucial role in mechanical homeostasis and mechanosensitive oncogenic signaling that drives hepatocarcinogenesis.
source: Here, we show that plectin, a major cytoskeletal crosslinker protein, plays a crucial role in mechanical homeostasis and mechanosensitive oncogenic signaling that drives hepatocarcinogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the entire study including genetic models, cell line experiments, and patient data analysis.

claim: Genetic and pharmacological inactivation of plectin potently suppressed the initiation and growth of HCC in autochthonous and orthotopic mouse models.
source: Using autochthonous and orthotopic mouse models we demonstrated that genetic and pharmacological inactivation of plectin potently suppressed the initiation and growth of HCC.
evidence: Supported by data from DEN-induced and Myc;sgTp53 mouse models shown in Figures 2 and 7.

claim: Plectin targeting potently inhibited the invasion potential of human HCC cells and reduced their metastatic outgrowth in the lung.
source: Moreover, plectin targeting potently inhibited the invasion potential of human HCC cells and reduced their metastatic outgrowth in the lung.
evidence: Supported by invasion assays (Figure 6A-E) and lung colonization experiments (Figure 6G-I).

claim: Proteomic and phosphoproteomic profiling linked plectin-dependent disruption of cytoskeletal networks to attenuation of oncogenic FAK, MAPK/Erk, and PI3K/Akt signatures.
source: Proteomic and phosphoproteomic profiling linked plectin-dependent disruption of cytoskeletal networks to attenuation of oncogenic FAK, MAPK/Erk, and PI3K/Akt signatures.
evidence: Supported by MS-based proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: Plectin inhibitor plecstatin-1 (PST) is well-tolerated and potently inhibits HCC progression in cell line-based and murine HCC models.
source: Importantly, by combining cell line-based and murine HCC models, we show that plectin inhibitor plecstatin-1 (PST) is well-tolerated and potently inhibits HCC progression.
evidence: Supported by PST treatment experiments in cell lines (Figures 2, 4, 5, 6) and mouse models (Figures 6, 7).

claim: Plectin-controlled cytoarchitecture is a key determinant of HCC development.
source: In conclusion, our study demonstrates that plectin-controlled cytoarchitecture is a key determinant of HCC development and suggests that pharmacologically induced disruption of mechanical homeostasis may represent a new therapeutic strategy for HCC treatment.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the entire study including cytoskeletal analyses (Figure 4) and functional assays.

claim: Pharmacologically induced disruption of mechanical homeostasis may represent a new therapeutic strategy for HCC treatment.
source: In conclusion, our study demonstrates that plectin-controlled cytoarchitecture is a key determinant of HCC development and suggests that pharmacologically induced disruption of mechanical homeostasis may represent a new therapeutic strategy for HCC treatment.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on PST treatment results throughout the study.

claim: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary malignancy of the liver and is a heterogeneous tumor entity with high metastatic potential and complex pathophysiology.
source: The most common primary malignancy of the liver, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), is a heterogeneous tumor entity with high metastatic potential and complex pathophysiology.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about HCC.

claim: Increasing evidence suggests that tissue mechanics plays a critical role in tumor onset and progression.
source: Increasing evidence suggests that tissue mechanics plays a critical role in tumor onset and progression.
evidence: This is a statement of emerging scientific consensus.

claim: Tumor progression is typically associated with a pathological increase of tissue stiffness caused by excessive deposition, crosslinking, and aberrant organization of dense extracellular matrix (ECM) fibers.
source: Tumor progression is typically associated with a pathological increase of tissue stiffness caused by excessive deposition, crosslinking, and aberrant organization of dense extracellular matrix (ECM) fibers.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: Increasing tissue rigidity drives tumor invasion and malignancy and correlates with poor patient survival.
source: Increasing tissue rigidity drives tumor invasion and malignancy and correlates with poor patient survival (Broders-Bondon et al., 2018; Piersma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tumor and stromal cells respond to altered mechanical properties of the extracellular milieu by translating physical cues into mechanosensitive signaling pathways.
source: At the cellular level, both tumor and stromal cells respond to altered mechanical properties of the extracellular milieu by translating physical cues into mechanosensitive signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in mechanobiology.

claim: Integrin-mediated adhesion induces the activation of FAK, MAPK/Erk, and PI3K/Akt pathways, leading to increased cell survival, migration, and invasion.
source: Integrin-mediated adhesion induces the activation of FAK, MAPK/Erk, and PI3K/Akt pathways, leading to increased cell survival, migration, and invasion (Cooper and Giancotti, 2019; Hoxhaj and Manning, 2020; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Plectin is a well-established regulator of cellular tensional homeostasis and mechanotransduction.
source: The best-studied example, a prototypical cytolinker plectin is a well-established regulator of cellular tensional homeostasis and mechanotransduction (Prechova et al., 2023) which is upregulated in various tumors (Gundesli et al., 2023; Perez et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Plectin is upregulated in various tumors.
source: The best-studied example, a prototypical cytolinker plectin is a well-established regulator of cellular tensional homeostasis and mechanotransduction (Prechova et al., 2023) which is upregulated in various tumors (Gundesli et al., 2023; Perez et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Through its canonical actin-binding domain (ABD) and intermediate filament (IF)-binding domain (IFBD), plectin crosslinks actin with IF networks and recruits them to cell adhesions, including FAs.
source: Through its canonical actin-binding domain (ABD; Andrä et al., 1998) and intermediate filament (IF)-binding domain (IFBD; Nikolic et al., 1996), plectin crosslinks actin with IF networks and recruits them to cell adhesions, including FAs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature describing plectin domains.

claim: Plectin deletion or mutation results in cytoskeletal reconfiguration accompanied by altered mechanical properties, such as cellular stiffness, stress propagation, and traction force generation.
source: Plectin deletion or mutation results in cytoskeletal reconfiguration accompanied by altered mechanical properties, such as cellular stiffness, stress propagation, and traction force generation (Eisenberg et al., 2013; Na et al., 2009; Osmanagic-Myers et al., 2015; Prechova et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Plectin-dependent changes in cell adhesions and cytoskeletal tension are associated with aberrant integrin-mediated mechanosignaling.
source: In addition, plectin-dependent changes in cell adhesions (Prechova et al., 2022; De Pascalis et al., 2018; Gregor et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020) and cytoskeletal tension (Osmanagic-Myers et al., 2015; Prechova et al., 2022; Gregor et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020; Marks et al., 2022) are associated with aberrant integrin-mediated mechanosignaling (Gregor et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Multiple reports have linked plectin with tumor malignancy.
source: Although multiple reports have linked plectin with tumor malignancy (Perez et al., 2021a) and other pathologies (Prechova et al., 2023; Vahidnezhad et al., 2022), mechanistic insights into how plectin functionally contributes to carcinogenesis remain largely unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Up to 90% of HCC cases occur on a background of liver fibrosis or cirrhosis, suggesting a causal link between increased deposition of ECM components and liver carcinogenesis.
source: Up to 90% of HCC cases occur on a background of liver fibrosis or cirrhosis, suggesting a causal link between increased deposition of ECM components and liver carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement of established clinical knowledge with an inference about causality.

claim: Plectin mRNA has been found to be upregulated in liver carcinomas, especially in the later stages of disease.
source: Consistent with this idea, plectin mRNA has been found to be upregulated in liver carcinomas, especially in the later stages of disease (Gundesli et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Changes in the interactions between the cytoskeleton and ECM may be important in HCC progression, particularly during the transition from local to metastatic malignancy.
source: Thus, changes in the interactions between the cytoskeleton and ECM may be important in HCC progression, particularly during the transition from local to metastatic malignancy.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the context provided.

claim: PLEC expression in publicly available datasets was significantly associated with gene signatures related to 'cell survival and proliferation', 'angiogenesis', and 'hypoxia'.
source: Strikingly, PLEC expression in publicly available datasets was significantly associated with gene signatures related to "cell survival and proliferation", "angiogenesis", and "hypoxia" (Figure 7—figure supplement 3) indicating that the PLEC mRNA level was associated with more aggressive cancer traits in HCC patients.
evidence: Supported by gene signature analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: PLEC expression levels were associated with TNM staging, underscoring plectin's prognostic value for HCC patient survival.
source: In addition, PLEC expression levels were associated with TNM staging, underscoring plectin's prognostic value for HCC patient survival.
evidence: Supported by TNM classification analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Loss of vimentin filament-FA linkage upon plectin deletion in highly migratory dermal fibroblasts was shown to uncouple the activation of FAK from actomyosin-generated tension and attenuate downstream effectors such as Src, Erk1/2, and p38.
source: Loss of vimentin filament-FA linkage upon plectin deletion in highly migratory dermal fibroblasts was shown to uncouple the activation of FAK from actomyosin-generated tension and attenuate downstream effectors such as Src, Erk1/2, and p38 (Gregor et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Plectin-dependent effects on PI3K/Akt and FAK/Erk signaling were recently described for prostate cancer and head and neck squamous carcinoma cells.
source: It is noteworthy that plectin-dependent effects on PI3K/Akt and FAK/Erk signaling were recently described for prostate cancer (Katada et al., 2012; Wenta et al., 2022) and head and neck squamous carcinoma cells (Burch et al., 2013), indicating that these observations have broader implications beyond liver cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Current systemic therapies for advanced HCC rely on a combination of multikinase inhibitors (such as sorafenib) or anti-VEGF antibodies/VEGF inhibitors (such as bevacizumab) treatment with immunotherapy.
source: Current systemic therapies for advanced HCC rely on a combination of multikinase inhibitors (such as sorafenib) or anti-VEGF antibodies/VEGF inhibitors (such as bevacizumab) treatment with immunotherapy (Cappuyns et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a statement of current clinical practice supported by citation.

claim: Multikinase inhibitors provide only moderate survival benefit due to primary resistance and the plasticity of signaling networks.
source: Multikinase inhibitors provide only moderate survival benefit (Llovet et al., 2018; Llovet et al., 2008) due to primary resistance and the plasticity of signaling networks (Yau et al., 2008), and only a subset of patients benefit from the addition of immunotherapy in HCC treatment (Yau et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Only a subset of patients benefit from the addition of immunotherapy in HCC treatment.
source: Multikinase inhibitors provide only moderate survival benefit (Llovet et al., 2018; Llovet et al., 2008) due to primary resistance and the plasticity of signaling networks (Yau et al., 2008), and only a subset of patients benefit from the addition of immunotherapy in HCC treatment (Yau et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PST was well-tolerated by mice and human cells, suggesting good potential for clinical utilization.
source: Similar to other ruthenium-based metallodrugs (Bakewell et al., 2018; Burris et al., 2016; Flocke et al., 2016), PST was well-tolerated by mice and human cells, suggesting good potential for clinical utilization.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations in the study and comparison to other ruthenium-based drugs cited.

claim: PST treatment closely mimics phenotypes fostered by ablation of the plectin gene.
source: We and others have previously demonstrated that PST treatment closely mimics phenotypes fostered by ablation of the plectin gene (Prechova et al., 2022; Meier et al., 2017; Meier-Menches et al., 2019; Wernitznig et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PST-mediated inhibition of plectin attenuates FAK, MAPK/Erk, and PI3K/Akt pathways in HCC cells with efficacy comparable to CRISPR/Cas-9-engineered functional (ΔIFBD) or full (KO) knockouts.
source: Consistently, PST-mediated inhibition of plectin attenuates FAK, MAPK/Erk, and PI3K/Akt pathways in HCC cells with efficacy comparable to CRISPR/Cas-9-engineered functional (ΔIFBD) or full (KO) knockouts.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and proteomic analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: Despite high PST target selectivity for plectin, the data do not rule out pleiotropic effects of PST in the liver.
source: However, despite high PST target selectivity for plectin (Meier-Menches et al., 2019), our data do not rule out pleiotropic effects of PST in the liver and further studies will be required to investigate whether PST mode-of-action in HCC entails molecular mechanisms other than engaging prooncogenic signaling cascades.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement acknowledging limitations, with citation to prior work on PST selectivity.
